query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A minor alloying addition of titanium (approximately 1 atomic %) into the CoCrFeNi matrix will promote the in situ formation of a fine, stable oxide tribolayer (likely a spinel-type oxide) during sliding that maintains a low coefficient of friction and wear rate from room temperature to 800 °C, relative to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-processed equiatomic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without additional modifying elements.
generation.intervention: Introduce a trace amount of Ti (~1 at%) into the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests under identical conditions at room temperature, intermediate (e.g., 400 °C) and high (800 °C) temperatures using similar applied loads (e.g., ~1 N) and sliding speeds in an ambient air environment.
generation.structural_mediator: In situ formation of a nanocrystalline, protective oxide tribolayer (potentially a spinel phase) enabled by the Ti addition.
generation.mechanism: The Ti addition is expected to accelerate tribo-oxidation such that during sliding, a continuous and adherent oxide layer forms on the alloy surface. At high temperatures, this oxide layer minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact, thereby reducing friction and wear. At room temperature, the modification does not adversely affect the underlying mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, the Ti-modified alloy should exhibit a consistently lower COF and reduced wear rate across the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The unmodified CoCrFeNi alloy, which demonstrates low friction and wear at room temperature but deteriorates (increased friction and wear) at elevated temperatures due to uncontrolled oxide formation.
generation.boundary: Temperature range: Room temperature to 800 °C; Applied sliding load around 1 N; Sliding speed and contact conditions maintained constant; Ambient air environment.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal Ti content and the durability/stability of the in situ formed oxide tribolayer under cyclic or prolonged sliding remain uncertain, as does the exact nature of the oxide phase.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set of standard CoCrFeNi alloy and one set modified with ~1 at% Ti. Subject both sets to controlled sliding wear tests at room temperature, 400 °C, and 800 °C under identical loads and sliding speeds. Use surface characterization techniques to verify the presence and continuity of the oxide tribolayer.
measurements: Coefficient of friction via in situ friction measurement
Quantitative wear rate (volume loss per N·m)
Surface oxide phase identification using XRD and SEM/EDS analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-modified samples do not display a statistically significant reduction and constancy in COF and wear rate across the temperature range compared to the unmodified samples, or if no continuous protective oxide layer is detected on the Ti-modified alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How does the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy change under reciprocating wear conditions at elevated temperatures, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
